ambient: Music built on atmosphere and texture rather than rhythm or melody: slow, spacious sound meant to be heard in the background as much as listened to. It took shape in the 1970s.
ambient techno: Techno with ambient textures: a steady but understated beat at slower tempos, built for home listening, often melodic or emotive.
chillstep: A calm, melodic offshoot of dubstep with ambient and chillout colours: half-time beats, soft pads and emotional melodies.
disco: Dance music of the 1970s built on a steady four-on-the-floor beat, a prominent bassline, strings and brass, and groove-heavy vocals.
dark psytrance:
Tempo: about 140-180 BPM.
A nocturnal, unsettling kind of psychedelic trance where mood matters more than melody. Eerie atmospheres, heavy basslines and sometimes glitchy, intricate rhythms sit on bold sound design that draws on minimal, industrial and dark ambient music. Horror-film samples and an alien feel are common, and the pace can run well past ordinary psytrance speed. The style took shape at the end of the 1990s.
downtempo: Relaxed electronic music at a slow to moderate pace, with a laid-back beat and warm, atmospheric sound. It grew out of the chillout scene of the 1990s.
drum and bass:
Tempo: about 160-180 BPM.
Fast electronic dance music from the 1990s: breakbeats at around 160 to 180 beats per minute over deep sub-bass lines.
forest psytrance:
Tempo: about 140-160 BPM.
An earthy, intricate kind of psychedelic trance with a dark mood like dark psytrance but a more organic sound and stronger resonance. Swarming effects, tribal percussion and natural samples such as animal calls, birdsong, rustling leaves and running water fill the mix. Melodies are simple and repetitive, mostly in minor scales, with few breakdowns. A slower strand known as swamp rarely goes above 135 BPM.
full-on psytrance:
Tempo: about 145-150 BPM.
Faster and more intense psytrance driven by harder rolling basslines: two or three 16th-note bass hits per bar, each cut off after the kick. Vocal samples and spacey effects ride on top, and melodic basslines that leap across several octaves are also frequent. It comes in a bright, uplifting morning flavour and a darker, more synthetic, cyberpunk night flavour, also called twilight psytrance. It is one of the most popular psytrance styles.
goa trance:
Tempo: about 135-150 BPM.
Goa trance is a psychedelic electronic style shaped by rapid, rolling arpeggios, driving basslines, and layered melodies that build into long, hypnotic journeys. Its synth lines often draw on Indian and other South Asian scales, while filter sweeps, distortion, and swirling effects create a vivid, hallucinatory atmosphere. Compared with later psytrance, classic Goa often has a warmer, more organic analogue sound. Tracks may weave in samples and imagery from mythology, science fiction, fantasy, or psychedelic culture. Rooted in Goa’s 1990s dance scene, the style remains known for its intricate arrangements, expansive builds, and sense of color and motion.
hi-tech psytrance:
Tempo: about 160-200 BPM.
Extremely fast psytrance that mixes dark psytrance and full-on elements. Glitchy, jittering sound design and complex rolling basslines that keep changing within a track make it dense and chaotic, yet the production stays clean and clear. The feel is lighter and bouncier than dark psytrance, with sharp, punchy percussion, and tempos often pass 200 BPM.
house:
Tempo: about 120-130 BPM.
Steady 4/4 dance music on a four-on-the-floor kick with claps or snares on beats 2 and 4, hi-hat and percussion loops, a warm, soulful synth bass groove, repetitive chords, simple melodies, vocal samples and a swinging, feel-good groove. Releases span roughly 115-135 BPM but cluster around 123-125, the narrowest spread of any dance genre, which makes it easy to mix in long, DJ-friendly tracks. It grew out of disco in 1980s Chicago (the Warehouse, Frankie Knuckles, Roland machines, Italo disco and synthpop influences; first records around 1984), alongside New York garage house (Paradise Garage, Larry Levan), and spread worldwide in three broad waves: the classic Chicago, garage and acid sound, the European styles, and electro house with its offshoots.
detroit techno:
Tempo: about 125-140 BPM.
Techno from Detroit in the mid 1980s, shaped by Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, the Belleville Three. A futuristic, machine-made sound with soul: Kraftwerk and electro, funk and Chicago house fed into hypnotic drum-machine grooves, driving basslines, lush synth pads and strings, and melodies that are often emotional. A harder, more minimal second wave followed, led by Underground Resistance, Jeff Mills and Robert Hood.
garage house:
Tempo: about 118-126 BPM.
House style from Larry Levan's sets at the Paradise Garage in New York, rooted in disco, R&B, soul and funk with gospel, dub and some new wave mixed in; synth playing and Levan's studio work added dub-style delay, echo and reverb (the Peech Boys' "Don't Make Me Wait"), and François K. was influential. Where Chicago house was raw, dry and drum-machine driven, garage put melody and singing first, with gospel and soul vocals, piano and organ chords, a live-sounding bass and warm dub-style reverb; the Jersey Sound (Club Zanzibar, Movin' Records, Newark) put songwriting over beats with crisp syncopated hi-hats and minor-chord pads and dominated from the late 1980s, later Masters at Work (Kenny Dope, Louie Vega) and Strictly Rhythm Records carried it, with staccato piano riffs and synth stabs as 1990s hallmarks, and from the mid 1990s it was the template for UK garage.
neurofunk: A dark, technical style of drum and bass with heavy, twisting basslines, tight sound design and a cold, mechanical edge.
nitzhonot:
Tempo: about 145-160 BPM.
Nitzhonot, Hebrew for victories, is a fast, simplified offshoot of Goa trance that emerged in Israel in the mid-1990s, partly as a response to police raids on Full Moon gatherings. Loud, high-pitched laserkicks carry quick Eastern-style melodies, giving a catchy, easy-to-hum sound, while early tracks often leaned on booming basslines and cartoon samples. It took shape on compilations from labels such as Betachronic and DR Recordings, and Eyal Barkan's 1998 album Good Morning Israel sold exceptionally well. Easy production brought many weak releases, Israeli artists drifted toward full-on psytrance, Greece developed a harder, epic Greek Uplifting, and a layered revival followed in the late 2000s.
outrun: A synthwave subgenre named after the 1986 arcade game Out Run, tied to the retro 1980s look.
progressive house: A melodic, gradual style of house that builds slowly with layered synths and long transitions, usually at a mid-tempo pace. It emerged in the 1990s.
progressive psytrance:
Tempo: about 130-140 BPM.
A cleaner, slower and more restrained kind of psytrance, with a groove closer to minimal techno, tech house and house than to the usual driving rush. Early tracks were dark and stripped-down, while from the mid-2000s the sound grew lighter and more atmospheric. Production is polished and the pace leaves room for long, gradual builds.
psycore:
Tempo: about 200-400 BPM.
A form of dark psytrance from the early 2010s, close to hi-tech in speed and dense sound design but darker and more experimental. The sound is static and hypnotic: a single-pitch bassline pulsing in very fast note divisions, like a rumble, over light percussion with simple sine kicks and often no snares. Pads with heavy reverb and swirling layers build complex but atmospheric soundscapes that borrow from dark ambient, glitch, hardcore and speedcore. Tracks above 200 BPM are very common, and it is most popular in Latin America.
psytrance:
Tempo: about 140-150 BPM.
Psychedelic trance: energetic electronic music with pounding bass riffs, often acid-style 303 lines, and constant filter modulation. Tracks are layered and evolve in steps, with elements added or removed about every eight bars, and they usually run past six minutes. It grew out of Goa trance with a strong acid trance influence, and has since split into many styles and fusions.
singer-songwriter: A performer writing and singing their own songs, usually with just a guitar or piano; lyrics matter more than production. Includes the Russian author song (bard) tradition.
spacesynth: A melodic, synth-led strain of Italo disco from the early 1980s, with a steady dance beat, euphoric arpeggios and vocoder, mostly instrumental.
suomisaundi:
Tempo: about 140-150 BPM.
Suomisaundi, Finnish for Finnish sound and also called spugedelic trance, is a Finnish deviation of psytrance, rooted in the Goa trance that Finnish party collectives introduced in the early 1990s and taking shape by the mid-1990s. It prizes free-form experimentation and humor: organic, Goa-style grooves mix with humppa, techno, punk rock, breakbeat, spoken word, hip hop, industrial metal, folk, funky guitar, video game music and cheap vintage electronics. The word spuge means an alcoholic, and the drunken feel shows in lyrics and titles about everyday life. Pioneers such as Tim Thick and Exogenic Records helped it win fans in Australia, New Zealand, Japan and Russia.
synthwave: Electronic music inspired by 1980s film scores, arcade games and synth-pop, with analog-style synthesizers, drum machines and a nostalgic, cinematic mood.
techno:
Tempo: about 120-150 BPM.
Repetitive, machine-driven electronic dance music built on a steady kick drum and layered rhythms. It emerged in the 1980s.
trance:
Tempo: about 130-150 BPM.
Melodic electronic dance music with repeating, hypnotic phrases and long builds towards an emotional peak. It emerged in the 1990s.
zenonesque: An experimental, leftfield strand of progressive psytrance from the mid-2000s, built on clean, atmospheric production with funky and jazzy touches, acoustic sound design and playful melodies. It borrows from techno, especially the minimal techno and tech trance of the 2000s. The sound first appeared in the work of Australian producer Sensient, head of Zenon Records, whose debut album Blue Neevus inspired many others, and the name came from the head of Ektoplazm. It spread to Germany and Israel, with later artists such as Ryanosaurus, Dirty Hippy and Grouch adding new elements, and its styles range from mechanical and futuristic to lighter and atmospheric.
acid trance: Trance that adds squelching acid basslines to its evolving structures.
dream trance:
Tempo: about 130 BPM.
A slow, laid-back and carefree trance with a dreamlike sound. It has strong roots in progressive house and uses beats typical of Eurodance and dance-pop.
euro trance: A fusion of trance and Eurodance: fast tempos, more accessible grooves and structures, and simple, catchy melodies with vocals and saw synth leads.
hands up: Euro trance built on prominent, melodic supersaw leads and dance-pop hooks, with sidechained basslines and hard, powerful drums.
hard trance: A rave-oriented trance with faster, thumping rhythms and strong melody and bassline sections. It grew out of the first wave of Western European trance in the early 1990s.
progressive trance: A mix of progressive house and early trance from Western Europe in the early to mid-1990s: gradual development, atmospheric textures, restrained energy and subtle melodic progression.
tech trance: A style from the late 1990s with energetic percussion, loud kicks, filtered hi-hats and tribal drums. Sidechained, detuned, repetitive leads and raw, distorted sounds come from techno, hard trance and electro house.
uplifting trance:
Tempo: about 135-142 BPM.
Euphoric melodies, build-breakdown-anthem structures and frequent supersaws.
vocal trance:
Tempo: about 120-145 BPM.
Melodic, polished, pop-like trance centred on vocals. It often overlaps with progressive, uplifting and Euro trance.
